title: How Pollen Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explain how pollen works, starting with a casual pollen-count banter about Atlanta and the pollen scale, then covering how plants evolved pollen (around 350 million years ago per the hosts' article), the look and shapes of pollen grains, the difference between gymnosperms (naked seed, e.g., pine cones) and angiosperms (flowering plants that protect seed in fruit), self- versus cross-pollination and the mechanisms plants use to avoid selfing, the stinky Devil's tongue and flower-animal co-evolution, and the complications GMO crops create for cross-pollination and patents. The episode closes with listener mail correcting a mix-up between propranolol and propofol from an earlier PTSD episode, a plug for the How Allergies Work episode, and sign-off. Includes ad reads for Audible and a message break.

segments.title: Opening banter and pollen count
segments.summary: Hosts joke about itchy sneezy edition and discuss Atlanta's pollen count of 39 (moderate) on the pollen scale, with peak counts near 9,000 and yellow-coated streets.

segments.title: Pollen's role in food and early plant evolution
segments.summary: Hosts note that about a third of foods come from pollinated plants and discuss bananas as sterile clones propagated by humans. They cover pollen's history, which predates bees, with plants spreading seed via pollen around 350 million years ago, and the purpose of pollen's shapes and wings.

segments.title: Phytonutrients and bitter plants
segments.summary: Discussion of phytonutrients, bitter taste and dandelion greens, and how food breeding moved toward sweeter, less bitter plants.

segments.title: Basics of pollination and flower anatomy
segments.summary: Explanation of pollination as the transfer of male pollen to the female ovule, with the pistil (ovary, style, stigma) and stamen (filament, anther) described.

segments.title: Gymnosperms vs. angiosperms and self-pollination
segments.summary: The two main plant groups are defined: gymnosperms (naked seed) and angiosperms (seed protected by fruit or shell). The hosts describe dandelion self-pollination and the mechanisms plants use to avoid self-pollinating, such as timing differences, separate male and female plants, biochemical blocking, and corn's timing mismatch, with peanuts as self-pollinators.

segments.title: How conifers like pine cones reproduce
segments.summary: Lodgepole pine example: male and female cones, sticky female cones, pollen tubes fertilizing ovules, and seeds released unprotected and dispersed by birds and other animals.

segments.title: Flowers, animal pollinators, and pollen grain formation
segments.summary: Angiosperm flowers attract bees, birds, bats and other animals with color, scent and nectar; examples include bumblebee and foxglove, Darwin's orchid prediction, and fruit dispersal by animals. Pollen formation from meiosis and the two sperm cells in angiosperm pollen, with endosperm nourishing the seedling, are covered.

segments.title: Devil's tongue and stinky pollination
segments.summary: Corpse-flower-like Sumatran plant that smells like decomposing flesh to attract carrion beetles, and the philodendron's heat-generated odor.

segments.title: GMO crops, cross-pollination and patents
segments.summary: Hosts discuss the conflict between GMO farmers, organic farmers and seed patent holders when pollen drifts between fields, including distance studies and crop-timing strategies.

segments.title: Listener mail: propranolol vs. propofol correction
segments.summary: A listener corrects the hosts' earlier mix-up of propranolol and propofol from the PTSD episode, explaining the drugs' differences and the risks of propofol.

segments.title: Sign-off and audible ad
segments.summary: Closing with contact options and a sponsor read for Audible.
